title: 2,000 Against 25,000: Did Nobunaga Really Win Okehazama by Sneaking Around the Hill?
description:
Late on the night of the 18th day of the 5th month of Eiroku 3 (1560), the Imagawa army had already marched into Owari. Yet in Kiyosu Castle, 27-year-old Oda Nobunaga said not a word about how to fight; he chatted until midnight and then sent his retainers home to bed.

Following the Shinchō Kōki, this episode walks with Nobunaga through that one day: Atsumori at dawn, the dash out of the castle with only five riders, the senior retainers grabbing his horse, a rain like hail that struck only the Imagawa army in the face, and the charge once the sky cleared. "Circling behind the hill for a surprise attack" and "drinking to victory in camp" were both added by later books; the last chapter covers who wrote that detour, and Yoshimoto's sword with its gold-inlaid inscription.

The Shinchō Kōki is quoted from the Meiji-era 我自刊我書 edition on Wikisource; Hoan's Shinchōki from the Genna 8 (1622) old movable-type edition, and the General Staff's Nihon Senshi: Okehazama from the Meiji 32 (1899) edition, both in the National Diet Library Digital Collections.

The source of every quotation, year and number is listed in the references below. Old-calendar dates are not converted, and sentences beginning "We think" are this channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone; modern researchers are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-19

chapters.night-castle: The night before the battle, Nobunaga sent everyone to bed
chapters.dawn-messenger: Atsumori at dawn, and a five-rider dash out of Kiyosu Castle
chapters.early-charge: The vanguard is routed; the elders grab Nobunaga's horse
chapters.sky-darkens: A rain that struck only the Imagawa army in the face
chapters.detour-book: A rewritten book and an army history drew the road behind the hill

ok101.text: The 18th day of the 5th month, Eiroku 3. Late at night, Kiyosu Castle.

ok102.text: The great Imagawa army from the east was in Owari.

ok103.text: His men waited for their 27-year-old lord, Oda Nobunaga, to say how to fight tomorrow.

ok104.text: Not one word about fighting. He chatted with them till midnight, then said: go to bed.

ok105.text: Walking out the gate, some sneered: his luck's run out, and so have his wits.

ok107.text: The next day, a downpour like hail struck only one side in the face.

ok108.text: Over 300 years later, Japan's Army General Staff mapped this battle.

ok109.text: And a sword survives to this day, with a line added to it.

ok110.text: That day, which road did he really take?

ok201.text: Remember "go to bed"? Before dawn, news arrived from the front.

ok202.text: Imagawa troops were besieging two border forts.

ok203.text: He stood up and danced a piece called Atsumori.

ok204.text: It goes: fifty years of human life, set against the heavens, are like a dream.

ok205.text: Then he shouted: Sound the conch! My armor!

ok206.text: He armored up, ate standing, put on his helmet and galloped out the gate.

ok207.text: Only five mounted pages followed him.

ok208.text: He left before the army had gathered.

ok217.text: Why he didn't talk tactics that night, the earliest detailed record doesn't say; it only tells what he did after dawn.

ok216.text: He rode over 10 km southeast in one go.

ok209.text: Around 7 or 8 a.m. he reached Atsuta; looking east, he saw smoke rising where the two forts stood.

ok210.text: By then, only about 200 foot soldiers had caught up.

ok215.text: At Zenshōji fort on the front, he gathered arriving troops and read the field.

ok212.text: For the Imagawa side, the earliest record says 45,000; today's common estimate is about 25,000.

ok213.text: Even the low count is over ten to one. Would he wait in the fort?

ok320.text: Seeing Nobunaga at Zenshōji, 300 men in front rushed at Yoshimoto.

ok314.text: Up on the hill, Yoshimoto won once more.

ok315.text: He said: not even demons or gods could stop my spearhead.

ok316.text: Then, unhurried, he had his camp sing utai.

ok326.text: Utai: the chant sung in Noh theater.

ok301.text: Nobunaga saw it. Instead of staying at Zenshōji, he pushed on to Nakajima, the frontmost fort.

ok302.text: His elders rushed to grab his reins.

ok303.text: They said: deep paddies line both sides; we'd have to go single file.

ok304.text: The enemy will see how few we are.

ok305.text: He ignored them and rode on.

ok306.text: The familiar version: Nobunaga slipped around the hill to hit from behind.

ok307.text: But in the earliest record, this is the road he took.

ok325.text: Against those odds, how to fight?

ok308.text: There he wanted to go further; the elders held him back hard.

ok309.text: They hauled food into Ōdaka Castle last night, then fought at the forts at dawn: up all night.

ok323.text: If they charge, fall back; if they fall back, chase.

ok312.text: Nobunaga added: take no heads. Cut them down and keep going.

ok313.text: Few as we are, fear not the great foe. Fortune lies with heaven.

ok322.text: He then led his men to the hill's base.

ok317.text: Later books say Yoshimoto drank to his victory in camp.

ok318.text: Earliest record: he rested his men at Mount Okehazama.

ok319.text: Yoshimoto didn't see the weather turning.

ok401.text: And turn it did. 5th month, old calendar: rainy season.

ok402.text: Suddenly a squall pelted down like stones, like ice.

ok404.text: It hit the Imagawa army in the face.

ok405.text: It hit the Oda army from behind.

ok406.text: A camphor two or three men could barely hug toppled east in the rain.

ok407.text: Men said: was this a divine army from the god of Atsuta?

ok408.text: Remember his boast about demons and gods?

ok409.text: What stopped him first was the rain.

ok410.text: The rain stopped; the sky cleared.

ok411.text: Spear in hand, Nobunaga yelled: Go! Go!

ok412.text: Kicking up dust like black smoke, the Oda army charged.

ok413.text: The Imagawa army scattered back like splashed water.

ok414.text: They left even his lacquered palanquin.

ok423.text: Many tales say Yoshimoto was too fat to ride, hence the palanquin; in fact, a lacquered one marked high rank.

ok415.text: Nobunaga pointed: there's the main camp! Charge!

ok416.text: At first, 300 riders ringed Yoshimoto, falling back.

ok417.text: Clash after clash, only 50 riders remained.

ok420.text: First to fight Yoshimoto was Hattori Koheita.

ok418.text: In the end, Imagawa Yoshimoto, 42, died at the hands of Mōri Shinsuke.

ok421.text: Before dark, Nobunaga was back at Kiyosu Castle.

ok419.text: So where did that road behind the hill come from?

ok501.text: That road came from a man a generation after Nobunaga.

ok527.text: Writing this day down before him was Ōta Gyūichi, an archer turned Nobunaga's scribe. His book: the Shinchō Kōki.

ok502.text: Remember the road the enemy could see? That's the one he wrote.

ok503.text: Fifty or sixty years after the battle, a man named Oze Hoan rewrote Nobunaga's story.

ok504.text: It reads like a novel, adding scenes the original lacks.

ok505.text: The loop behind the hill and the rear attack first appear in this book.

ok506.text: Ōta's book stayed in manuscript; Hoan's was printed and sold early on.

ok525.text: In the Edo period, most ordinary readers read this one.

ok528.text: But how did one book's story become the answer everyone believed?

ok507.text: Remember the General Staff's map from the start?

ok508.text: In Meiji 32, the General Staff published Nihon Senshi: Okehazama, written for students of tactics.

ok509.text: Remember Hoan's road behind the hill? This book has the same one.

ok529.text: It even kept the scout's report that only Hoan had.

ok510.text: From Hoan to the General Staff the story carried on; after the army's book, it stayed the standard for 80-plus years.

ok511.text: Not until 1982 did a researcher closely reread the Shinchō Kōki,

ok512.text: arguing there was no detour raid.

ok526.text: Later studies also estimate the Imagawa army was spread across sites; Yoshimoto's own camp had far fewer.

ok513.text: Since then, a head-on charge once the rain stopped has been a strong theory; scholars still argue the details.

ok514.text: Remember that sword? It was Yoshimoto's own.

ok515.text: On the tang, hidden inside the hilt, a line is inlaid in gold, signed Oda Owari-no-kami Nobunaga.

ok517.text: But researchers note that in Eiroku 3 he went by Kazusa-no-suke, not Owari-no-kami; the Shinchō Kōki also calls him Kazusa-no-suke here.

ok518.text: The Agency for Cultural Affairs dates it to when Nobunaga got the sword. But the title doesn't fit: was it added later too?

ok524.text: We think the detour raid sounds good because it hands the few beating the many a clever reason.

ok520.text: Taiga drama, game or textbook: where'd you first meet Okehazama?

ok521.text: We only tell what the records hold. Subscribe to open the files with us.
